title: Get Started
intro: Learn how Codex, GitHub, and Cloudflare work together.
do: Learn how Codex, GitHub, and Cloudflare work together.

title: How DLL websites work
do:
Three tools work together. You can use them without becoming an expert in all three.

Already have a website? Open Find your website (Find your website before changing anything) and identify its GitHub repository, production branch, Cloudflare project, and live domain before making changes.

Starting a new website? Go to Create a New Website.

Need to update a live website? Go to Update an Existing Website.
understand:
Codex helps you make changes. You describe what you want, and Codex can help inspect a project, plan changes, edit files, and run checks. You still review its work and approve important actions.

GitHub keeps the website's source and change history. Each DLL website normally has its own repository (a project containing the website's code and related files). Proposed changes go through a review process before they become the approved version.

Cloudflare publishes the approved website. The lab's workflow connects the website's approved GitHub production branch to its Cloudflare deployment. Cloudflare builds and serves the website and may also manage domain/DNS settings.

Key point: Codex is the helper, GitHub is the authoritative source of the website, and Cloudflare publishes from the approved source. People remain responsible for reviewing changes and authorizing publication.
deep:
Repository: The complete set of source files needed to maintain the website. DLL uses GitHub as the authoritative copy; don't maintain a separate production copy manually in Cloudflare or ChatGPT Sites.

Production branch: The branch Cloudflare uses to publish the official version; normally main, but confirm the branch for your website.

Working branch: A separate line of changes so you can prepare and review updates before merging them into production.

Commit: A recorded change in the repository's history.

Pull request (PR): A request to review and merge changes from one branch into another. DLL production changes must go through a reviewed PR.

Deployment: The build and publication of a particular code version. Check that the deployed version matches the approved GitHub version.

Domain: The website's human-readable address, such as example.org. A subdomain might be project.example.org.

DNS: Records that tell internet services where to find the website and other domain services, including email. Changing nameservers affects more than the website; see the migration safeguards before doing so.

Domain registrar: The company where the domain is registered. Nameservers identify the service responsible for the domain's DNS records.

Worker/project: The named Cloudflare resource that hosts/deploys the website. Each DLL site should have its own uniquely named Cloudflare resource.

Important nuance: A branch or PR protects the review workflow, but changes merged into the production branch may trigger publishing automatically. Don't treat a merged PR as a harmless draft.

title: Get ready: access and permissions
do:
Before you begin, make sure you can reach the right tools and that you know who may approve changes. You may not need every type of access for every task.

Basic setup checklist

Only when applicable

Don't have access? Ask the website owner or the person who administers the lab's GitHub/Cloudflare access. Use your own Cloudflare account; do not ask someone to share the owner password. A Cloudflare administrator should invite you with permissions appropriate to the task.

Ready for the next step? Go to Find your website (Find your website before changing anything) or Build Your Website.
understand:
Why do these accounts matter? Your ChatGPT/Codex access lets you request assisted work; GitHub permissions determine whether you can contribute changes to a repository; Cloudflare permissions determine what hosting or domain resources you can manage. Publication may also require approval from a person responsible for the website.

Why separate logins? Individual Cloudflare accounts and appropriate member permissions reduce the risks of shared passwords and make access easier to manage. Maintainers must enable multi-factor authentication when they accept invitations.
deep:
Minimum access principle: Get only the permissions necessary to do your role. A Cloudflare Super Administrator invites maintainers through Manage Account → Members and assigns the relevant permissions. The maintainer accepts the invitation and enables multi-factor authentication.

Installing tools: Ask Codex to inspect the computer, explain anything missing, and request approval before installing software or opening sign-in pages. You do not need to configure website tools manually in advance.

Sensitive information: Do not put passwords, API keys, authentication/recovery codes, subscriber information, private research data, or unpublished research material into GitHub or Codex prompts. Use protected secrets/environment variables as appropriate; don't put their values into source files.

title: Find your website before changing anything
do:
Every DLL website has its own setup. Confirm the correct project first, especially if you help manage more than one website.

1. Locate your project

Open the website's project in Codex. If you don't know which repository or folder belongs to the website, ask the website owner before proceeding.

2. Ask Codex to inspect, not edit

Copyable prompt — verify an existing site

Verify that this folder is connected to the correct GitHub repository for <WEBSITE NAME>.

Identify the production branch, Cloudflare project or Worker, build commands, test commands, public domains, and current deployment workflow.

Do not change files, install software, commit, push, merge, deploy, or publish anything. Give me a plain-language summary of what you find.

3. Check the results

Compare the website's name, repository, branch, Cloudflare resource, and addresses with what the owner or lab documentation expects. Do not proceed if the project identity is unclear.

4. Keep a simple website record

Field Your website
Website name / purpose [fill in]
GitHub repository [fill in]
Production branch [fill in — normally main]
Cloudflare Worker / project [fill in]
Temporary Cloudflare address [fill in, if used]
Public domain and subdomains [fill in]
Website owner and publication approver [fill in]
Domain registrar [fill in]
Important forms / email / analytics / database [fill in]
Additional technical fields

Required runtime version; build and deploy commands; environment variable names; other external services; date of first verified production deployment; routine edit and rollback procedures.
understand: Why record these details? Two DLL websites may look similar but use different repositories, branches, Cloudflare resources, build commands, and domains. A correct change in the wrong repository is still the wrong change. Ask Codex to inspect and confirm details for each specific site.
deep:
Example only: WRITE AI Center (do not reuse these values blindly)

  • Repository: UCI-DLL/write-ai-center-website
  • Production branch: main
  • Cloudflare Worker: write-ai-website
  • Addresses: https://writeai.center and https://www.writeai.center

These values are examples. Another DLL site can have different build/test commands, domain names and deployment settings. Website records should be maintained with the repository's documentation; see Find the important details about my website for the complete field list.

title: Work safely: rules everyone should know
do:
You don't have to memorize technical commands. But everyone should understand the few habits that protect a live website and the people who use it.

Essentials

  1. Start with the right website. Confirm repository, production branch, Cloudflare project, and domains.
  2. Keep GitHub as the source of truth. Normal site edits go through GitHub, not direct changes to production files in the Cloudflare dashboard or an independent live copy.
  3. Review before publishing. Use a separate branch and reviewed pull request for meaningful changes. Check previews and testing results before approving anything.
  4. Don't share secrets. Keep passwords, tokens, recovery codes, subscriber data and private research out of repositories and Codex prompts.
  5. Protect existing services. DNS changes can disrupt email and other domain services; preserve DNS records and keep old hosting until migration is verified.
  6. Verify the actual live site. Test every intended public address, HTTPS, pages, links, images, downloads, forms and desktop/mobile layouts.
  7. Undo changes through GitHub. A bad publication should be addressed with a reviewed GitHub revert so GitHub and Cloudflare stay synchronized.
understand:
What's the main safety idea? We want one clear, reviewed history of what was published. That makes it easier to collaborate, test, and recover without overwriting other people's work.

What if Codex says the work is done? That is not the final check. An authorized person must verify the actual live website. If someone else's website is being moved or published, get the required approval first.
deep:
Repository and collaboration

  • Each website should normally have its own GitHub repository.
  • GitHub must contain the full authoritative source.
  • Each website must have a uniquely named Cloudflare Worker or project.
  • Document the production branch, normally main.
  • Use a separate working branch and reviewed PR for each meaningful change.
  • Ask Codex to preserve other people's work; never overwrite unfinished contributions.
  • Do not keep an independent production website in ChatGPT Sites or upload a separate production copy manually to Cloudflare.

Access and security

  • Use individual Cloudflare logins with appropriate member permissions; do not share the Cloudflare owner password.
  • Keep passwords, private keys, API tokens, subscriber information, recovery codes, and unpublished research materials out of GitHub and Codex prompts.
  • Store sensitive configuration in Cloudflare secrets or protected environment variables.
  • Get approval from the website owner before moving, replacing, or publishing a site.

Domain and migration safety

  • Review all DNS records before changing nameservers, especially email and domain-verification records.
  • Keep the former host available until migration is verified and approved; do not cancel it prematurely.
  • Ask Codex to check for dependencies including forms, analytics, databases and external services.

Testing, publication and recovery

  • Preview and test before publication.
  • Check live domains, HTTPS, desktop/mobile, navigation, images, links, downloads and forms.
  • Have Cloudflare publish the approved GitHub production branch.
  • Confirm that the deployed version is the approved repository version.
  • Use a GitHub revert for faulty production changes; review and test the revert before merging.
  • An update or migration is complete only after Codex reports successful checks and an authorized person independently verifies the live site.
  • Document website ownership, repository, deployment, domain, build commands, and routine procedures.

title: Build Your Website
intro: Create or update a website with Codex and GitHub.
do: Create or update a website with Codex and GitHub.

title: Start Exploring: Shape Your Website Idea
intro: Turn your idea into an informed design brief before coding.
do:
A good website begins with understanding the people who will use it. You don't have to know coding or design terminology to begin.

This is a thinking starter—not a complete website design brief. These questions help you notice key decisions and unanswered questions. They may not provide enough detail for a well-designed website. You can build on your answers in Develop Your Design Further before moving into technical creation.

Capture your first ideas

Respond to what you know now. It is fine to leave questions open or change your answers.

What next?

Develop your design further →Examine user needs, content, navigation, accessibility, and what success looks like.Already have a complete plan? Start building →Use your decisions to guide Codex through a reviewed development process.
understand:
Why think before coding?

Codex can help create pages quickly, but it cannot decide your audience's priorities for you. The questions on this page help you communicate who your website serves and what visitors should accomplish.

Flow A: Design the experience

People → Purpose → Key tasks → Content and navigation → Usability → Evidence of success

Decide what makes the experience useful.
Flow B: Build and publish

Design decisions → Codex → GitHub review → Cloudflare publication → Test and improve

Turn a thoughtful plan into a functioning website.

The initial answers here are a starting point. The deeper design guide helps you turn them into decisions you can actually evaluate.
deep:
What makes a design brief actionable?

An actionable brief describes specific audiences and tasks, the content needed, a proposed structure, example visitor journeys, design and accessibility constraints, integrations, ownership, and how you will evaluate success.

It can include unresolved questions, as long as they are identified rather than guessed. You may need conversations with stakeholders or actual users, a content inventory, and a simple prototype before a final brief is ready.

Continue to Develop Your Design Further →

title: Develop Your Design Further
intro: Turn first ideas into an actionable, user-centered design brief.
do:
This is a deeper planning path for anyone who wants to design a useful, accessible website before starting the technical work. You can begin here even if you skipped the short idea starter.

Outcome: A clearer design brief—not code. Work through the decisions that apply to your project; revisit them as you learn more.

1. Understand the people and context

  • Identify primary and secondary audiences, their goals, existing knowledge, and likely access needs.
  • Find out which questions and tasks matter most to them. When possible, ask a few representative visitors instead of assuming.
  • Consider mobile use, language, accessibility, and constraints such as time or connection speed.

2. Define the purpose and success

  • Write one sentence: “This website helps [audience] to [outcome].”
  • Choose the top two or three actions visitors should be able to accomplish.
  • Define observable evidence of success, such as a visitor locating a resource without help.

3. Plan content before pages

  • List what you already have: text, images, resources, links, approvals, forms, and downloadable files.
  • Identify missing content and who will provide or maintain it.
  • Group content by visitor needs; name sections using language that makes sense to visitors.

4. Sketch the visitor journey and navigation

  • Choose one common starting point and one realistic goal.
  • Sketch the path from arrival to completion. Can visitors recognize where to go next?
  • Make an initial sitemap; keep the top-level choices manageable and expose detail progressively.

5. Decide how people will interact

  • Choose where visitors should read, search, filter, compare, submit, or get feedback.
  • For educational websites, consider what learners will do or create—not only what they will read—and what guidance they need.
  • Use interactions because they improve the task, not simply because they look engaging.

6. Plan visual design and inclusion

  • Specify brand assets, tone, typography, color, layout, and examples.
  • Consider readability, keyboard access, focus states, labels, image alternatives, and responsive behavior.
  • Check that the most important actions remain apparent without relying on color alone.

7. Define technical needs and responsibilities

  • Identify forms, privacy expectations, analytics, logins, databases, email, integrations, domains, and redirects.
  • Decide who owns content, who reviews it, and who is allowed to approve publication.
  • Separate required features from nice-to-have ideas.

8. Review your concept before coding

  • Share the sitemap and rough page outline with someone unfamiliar with the site.
  • Ask them where they would go to complete important tasks. Revise confusing labels or steps.
  • Record open questions, acceptance criteria, and what should not change during implementation.

Prepare the handoff

Your refined brief should include audience, purpose, user tasks, content map, page structure, key journeys, interaction requirements, design and accessibility direction, technical needs, ownership, unresolved questions, and success criteria.

Return to the idea starter →Collect or revisit your initial answers.Create your website with Codex →Use the refined brief to request a plan, review it, then begin implementation.
understand:
Why these decisions matter

Design is about deliberately shaping what someone can understand and accomplish. A technically correct website can still be difficult to use when its labels, information order, or interactions don't reflect visitor needs.

Information architecture

Information architecture means how content is grouped, named, and connected. People should recognize where to go without needing to understand the website's internal organization.

Learning experience design

For learning-oriented sites, consider outcomes, authentic tasks, opportunities to apply ideas, useful feedback, and the ability to get more support or depth when needed.

Iteration

Design briefs are working agreements, not predictions. Testing a simple prototype may reveal important improvements before building the full website.
deep:
Further design methods

Audience evidence

Conduct a short interview or observation with a representative user. Look for real tasks and friction points rather than only asking what colors they prefer.

Task flows and content models

Map entry point → decision → action → result, including error and recovery states. Define reusable content types and ownership where content will need ongoing updates.

Accessible interactions

Design forms with explicit labels and errors, make controls usable with a keyboard, provide visible focus indications, avoid color-only meaning, and test small-screen navigation.

Evaluation plan

Write three realistic task scenarios. Observe whether users can complete them, where they hesitate, and which descriptions they misunderstand. Revise before production.

Technical handoff

Specify expected behavior, content, approved assets, security and privacy boundaries, integrations, responsive states, and acceptance tests. Ask Codex to identify assumptions and propose the technical architecture before implementation; human reviewers still authorize changes and publication.

Explore the related tools overview or proceed to Create a New Website.

title: Create a New DLL Website
do:
Have a design brief? If you want help shaping one, try Start Exploring to clarify audience, goals, visitor journey, and site structure. Both design paths are optional; you can begin with a plan you already have.

Start with an idea. Codex can help turn it into a working website. You'll check its plan, review a local preview, and then save the approved website in the right GitHub repository. You won't publish to the public web during this guide.

Step 1. Make a short website plan

Have ready:

  • Website name, purpose, and intended audience
  • Domain or subdomain you'd like to use
  • Proposed GitHub repository name and unique Cloudflare Worker/project name
  • Pages and features needed
  • Content owner and person authorized to approve publication
  • Whether the site needs forms, email, authentication, database, analytics, or other external services

Before continuing: The website must have its own clearly named GitHub repository and separate Cloudflare deployment. Do not put an unrelated DLL website inside another website's repository. Confirm the proposed names do not duplicate existing resources.

Quick help: Not sure what a repository is? Understand: website source and repository · Not sure what a domain is? Get Started / domains

Step 2. Ask Codex for a plan — before it builds

Create or open an empty, permanent project folder in Codex. Fill in the placeholders and copy this Codex prompt:

Help me create a new DLL website named <WEBSITE NAME>.

Its purpose is <PURPOSE>, its audience is <AUDIENCE>, and it needs these pages and features: <REQUIREMENTS>.

It will be stored in a new GitHub repository named <REPOSITORY NAME> under <APPROVED GITHUB ORGANIZATION>. It will be published through the shared DLL Cloudflare account using a unique Worker or project.

Check this computer for the required tools and ask for approval before installing software or opening sign-in pages.

First propose:

1. The site structure
2. The technology and framework
3. The accessibility approach
4. The testing plan
5. The GitHub repository plan
6. A unique Cloudflare Worker or project name
7. The preview and publishing workflow
8. Any expected costs or external services

Do not create, upload, deploy, purchase, or publish anything until I approve the plan.

You should see: A proposal, not a deployed website. Check its structure, technologies, costs, accessibility, tests, and ownership before approving work.

Good to know: Codex may inspect an approved existing DLL site as a technical example, but must not copy its branding, content, private information, or unnecessary code. Example reference: https://github.com/UCI-DLL/write-ai-center-website.

Step 3. Build a local version — not the public site

After you approve the proposal, copy:

Create the approved website locally.

Include clear setup instructions, a Cloudflare-compatible production configuration, appropriate automated checks, and a sample environment file containing variable names only, never secret values.

Run the website locally and inspect every page at desktop and mobile sizes. Do not create the GitHub repository, connect Cloudflare, or publish anything yet.

Provide Codex with the approved website text, images, logos, links, contact details, required disclaimers, accessibility requirements, and privacy information. Do not use copyrighted or unapproved material.

You should see: A local working preview you can inspect before it goes onto GitHub.

Step 4. Review the website before saving it

Once the local site looks complete, copy:

Run all available build, test, lint, accessibility, and link checks.

Show me the final local preview and a plain-language inventory of the website. Identify any unfinished content, placeholder links, missing images, broken interactions, or external services that still require configuration.

Do not publish anything.

Check yourself: Every page exists; navigation and links work; images and downloads are correct; desktop and mobile versions look good; forms and interactions behave as expected; placeholders and unfinished services have been identified. Ask Codex to correct problems and preview again before approval.

Step 5. Prepare the GitHub repository

After the local website is approved, copy:

Prepare to create the approved GitHub repository under <GITHUB ORGANIZATION>.

Confirm that generated files, dependencies, logs, local environment files, credentials, and secrets will be excluded. Show me the proposed repository name, description, visibility, default branch, and initial files.

Do not create or upload anything until I approve.

Check yourself: Correct approved organization; clear repository name; proposed visibility and branch; no credentials, secrets, logs, or generated dependencies included. Then authorize creation with the next prompt.

Step 6. Create the repository and request review

After you approve the repository plan, copy:

Create the approved GitHub repository. Commit the complete website source to a separate branch and open a pull request for its initial review.

Do not merge or publish it yet. Give me the repository address, review link, and check results.

Review and approve the pull request. Merge into main or the documented production branch only when the source is ready and the authorized review is complete.

At this point: Your approved website source is in GitHub. It is not necessarily publicly available yet. Continue to Publish Your Website → Connect GitHub to Cloudflare; test temporary deployment; choose domain setup; publish and verify.
understand:
Codex is the builder's assistant, not the final approver. You describe the site, Codex proposes a plan and creates a local version, and you inspect the result before allowing it to be stored or published.

Local preview vs. live website: A local preview lets you assess work without changing what public visitors see. Publishing happens later when the approved GitHub production branch is deployed through Cloudflare.

Why create a repository only after reviewing a local build? The new-site workflow separates planning, building, approval, GitHub review, and publishing into checkpoints. The point is to avoid accidental publication and to make changes reviewable.

What is a pull request? A request to review a proposed set of code changes before merging it into the approved branch. It offers a chance to check what will become the official source.

Why ask about forms and databases at the beginning? A brochure site and a site that collects submissions can need different services, configuration, privacy safeguards, and maintenance plans.
deep:
• Project architecture: Framework, build process, runtime version, Cloudflare-compatible production configuration.
  • Quality: Build checks, tests, linting, accessibility, links, mobile/responsive testing.
  • Configuration: Sample environment file lists names only; real credentials should not go into the repository or Codex prompts.
  • Git history: Separate feature branch → commit → pull request → review → merge into approved production branch.
  • Deployment boundary: The new site is not considered complete because a local preview or GitHub repository exists; the publishing guide covers the Cloudflare connection and verification.
  • Approved reference site: WRITE AI Center UCI-DLL/write-ai-center-website is an example only, not a universal template or build command set.

Next: Publish an Approved Update. Need help? Deployment failed · Recover a faulty publication.

title: Update an Existing DLL Website
do:
Need to replace an image, change wording, add a page, or adjust a layout? Work on a safe copy, check the preview, and request review before publishing anything.

Step 1. Open and verify the correct website

Open the website's local project folder in Codex. Paste:

Verify that this folder is connected to the correct GitHub repository for <WEBSITE NAME>.

Identify the production branch, Cloudflare project or Worker, build commands, test commands, public domains, and current deployment workflow.

Do not change files, install software, commit, push, merge, deploy, or publish anything. Give me a plain-language summary of what you find.

Stop and check: Did Codex identify the right website, repository, production branch, project, and domain? The WRITE AI Center repository https://github.com/UCI-DLL/write-ai-center-website is a example, not the repository for every site.

Step 2. Prepare a safe working branch

Copy:

Prepare this website for a new change. Check for unfinished or uncommitted work, safely obtain the newest approved production version from GitHub, and create a separate branch for this request.

Preserve other people’s work. Do not edit, commit, push, merge, deploy, or publish anything yet. Tell me when it is safe to begin.

Stop and check: Wait until Codex says it is safe to proceed. If it finds unfinished work or changes made by someone else, don't overwrite them.

Step 3. Describe and approve the change

Describe in plain language:

  • Which page should change
  • Exact wording (if applicable)
  • Images/files to use and links to add
  • Desired placement and styling
  • Anything that must remain unchanged

Then copy:

Review this request against the existing website design and structure.

Explain what you plan to change, which files will be affected, and any accessibility, mobile-layout, data, form, or content risks. Wait for my approval before editing.

Stop and check: Read the proposed changes. If the plan looks correct, explicitly approve Codex making the change.

Step 4. Preview and test before GitHub review

Copy:

Check this change completely. Run all build, test, lint, accessibility, and validation commands already provided by the repository.

Open the local preview and inspect the affected page at desktop and mobile sizes. Also verify navigation, images, links, forms, and the other public pages.

Show me the preview and give me a plain-language summary of every file changed. Do not commit, push, merge, deploy, or publish anything.

Important: Each site can have different check commands. Codex must read the repository documentation/configuration instead of assuming the same commands work everywhere.

Example only, for WRITE AI Center: npm run build, npm test, npm run lint.

You check: Open the preview yourself; look at both desktop and mobile. If something is wrong, tell Codex plainly and ask it to run the checks again. Example for this process:

The image is cropped too closely on mobile. Correct that issue, rerun the relevant checks, and show me the updated preview. Do not publish.

Repeat until the change is correct.

Step 5. Open a pull request for review

Once you're satisfied with the preview, copy:

I approve the local change. Save only the files related to this request, commit them on the separate branch, push the branch to GitHub, and open a pull request for review.

Do not merge the pull request or publish the change. Give me the review link, the check results, and a short summary of the change.

Share the review link with the authorized reviewer. Each meaningful change should have its own pull request.

Step 6. Publish the approved change

Publication requires separate approval. Follow Publish an Approved Update only when the pull request and release are approved.

After the pull request is approved, copy:

This pull request is approved.

Confirm that all required checks passed, merge it into the documented production branch, and monitor the Cloudflare production deployment.

When publishing finishes, verify that the deployed Git commit matches the merged GitHub commit. Test the changed page, navigation, images, links, forms, HTTPS, desktop layout, and mobile layout.

Report the final GitHub commit and all live website addresses.

Verify yourself: Open every official live address and inspect the updated page. For the WRITE AI Center example, this includes both https://writeai.center and https://www.writeai.center. Don't consider the update finished until Codex reports success and you have checked the live page personally.
understand:
Why check the repository first? Working on the wrong project can affect the wrong site. A correct project identity includes the repository, production branch, Cloudflare deployment, and public addresses.

Why a separate branch? It keeps the proposed change apart from the official approved version until review.

Why review the preview? Codex can make changes and run tests, but people still need to judge wording, visual quality, and whether the result matches the request.

What happens after the pull request? Approval and merge update the GitHub production branch. Cloudflare Workers Builds can be configured to automatically build and deploy changes on that branch; preview builds for other branches may also be enabled.

What does 'source of truth' mean? GitHub is the complete authoritative source. Do not update production files directly in the Cloudflare dashboard or maintain an independent live copy in ChatGPT Sites.
deep:
• Uncommitted work and collaborators: Detect and preserve work that hasn't yet been safely committed; don't force-push or overwrite another person's changes.
  • Change boundaries: Commit only files related to the task; use a separate pull request for each meaningful change.
  • Validation: Build, test, lint, accessibility, and other repository-defined checks vary by website.
  • Deployment chain: Approved PR → documented production branch → Cloudflare production deployment → compare deployed commit with merged commit → verify public domains.
  • Production vs. preview deployments: Some Workers Builds setups support automatic production and separate preview builds, depending on configuration.
  • Recovery: A failed deployment or faulty public change should be addressed through the GitHub workflow, not by manually publishing a different copy.

Next: Publish an Approved Update. Need help? Deployment failed · Recover a faulty publication.

title: Build & Edit: Quick Reference
do:
What should I put in a Codex request?

State the goal, the affected page or feature, exact replacement text, approved assets and links, desired placement, and what must not change. For consequential tasks, have Codex explain its plan first and wait for approval. Never put passwords, API keys, private research data, authentication codes, recovery codes, or subscriber information into prompts or GitHub.

Before you approve a change

  1. Correct website/repository and correct responsible people?
  2. Approved content and assets, with necessary accessibility/privacy requirements?
  3. No secrets or unapproved materials in repository or prompt?
  4. Plan clearly scoped, including any risks to mobile, forms, data, or links?
  5. Local preview examined personally, with available checks passing?
  6. PR opened and reviewed before merging into production?
  7. Public deployment and every official domain verified when publishing is complete?

I need help with…

  • Find the correct website project
  • Protect unfinished work and prepare a safe branch
  • Keep a change within the approved scope
  • Preview, test and fix mobile layout
  • Find why a website update is not live
  • Diagnose a failed deployment
  • Recover a faulty publication
  • Move an existing website to Cloudflare
understand:
Why this matters

This task is part of the shared DLL workflow: Codex helps prepare or inspect work, GitHub keeps the approved website source and review history, and Cloudflare publishes the approved production branch. Use the steps in Do It when ready, and review the checks and approvals before changing anything public.
deep:
Technical context

Every DLL website can have its own repository, build commands, branch, Cloudflare project, domain records, and connected services. Before applying a technical instruction, confirm those details for this particular site. Keep credentials and unpublished sensitive information out of prompts and the repository. When a change affects shared services, review the impact and rollback plan before approval.

title: Publish Your Website
do: Bring a site online safely.

title: Publish a New Website
do:
Your finished website is in its approved GitHub repository. Let's connect it to Cloudflare and give it a public address.

Before you start

Confirm that the site has been built and reviewed locally; all available checks have run; its complete, approved source is in a dedicated GitHub repository; and its reviewed pull request has been merged into the documented production branch (normally main). Confirm who owns the site and has publication authority. Know the approved project name and whether you'll use a subdomain of a DLL domain or a new root domain. Do not put credentials or secrets in GitHub or a Codex prompt.

Step 1 — Prepare the Cloudflare setup

Open the correct project in Codex. Ask Codex to propose the deployment first—not create it immediately.

Copyable Codex prompt

Prepare a new Cloudflare deployment for this repository using the approved unique name.

Configure Cloudflare Builds so that the approved GitHub production branch is the production source.

Show me:

    1. The proposed Cloudflare product
    2. The build command
    3. The deploy command
    4. The required runtime version
    5. The repository connection
    6. The production branch
    7. The environment variables and secrets
    8. The expected temporary address
    9. Any Cloudflare settings or resources that will be created

Do not create or connect anything until I approve it.

Check before approving: Correct repository and production branch? Distinct Worker/project name? Expected configuration and any external services accounted for? Cloudflare shared account access through your own member login (do not share owner password)?

Step 2 — Deploy to a temporary address

Once the proposed setup is reviewed and approved:

Create the approved Cloudflare deployment and GitHub connection.

Deploy the current production branch to the temporary Cloudflare address, wait for the deployment to finish, and test the complete website.

Do not connect a public domain yet.

What to do yourself: Open the temporary address; test pages, navigation, images, downloads, links, forms, desktop and mobile layout. If anything fails, resolve it before exposing the public domain.

Step 3 — Choose the correct domain path

A. Using a subdomain of an existing DLL domain (such as project.example.org): If the root domain already uses Cloudflare nameservers, do not change the nameservers. Confirm domain owner approval and check whether the desired hostname is already used by a record, redirect, route, or other service. Add the approved subdomain as a Cloudflare Custom Domain for the project only after checking for conflicts and getting approval.

Prepare to connect <SUBDOMAIN> to <CLOUDFLARE PROJECT>.

Check for existing DNS records, redirects, Worker routes, certificates, or other services using this hostname. Show me the exact proposed change and its rollback procedure.

Do not save the change until I approve it.

B. Using an entirely new root domain (such as example.org): Get approval before purchasing/registering the domain. After registration, add it to the shared DLL Cloudflare account using full DNS setup, review imported DNS records, change the registrar's nameservers to those assigned by Cloudflare, wait for the zone to become Active, and connect root and www hostnames to the approved deployment. If there is any pre-existing website, email, or other domain service, follow the full migration safeguards in Move an Existing Website to Cloudflare rather than the shorter new-domain path.

Step 4 — Approve publication and verify the live site

After the temporary site works and the domain plan has been reviewed, issue the final publication instruction:

I approve the public-domain connection.

Connect <DOMAIN> and, if required, <WWW.DOMAIN> to the approved Cloudflare deployment.

Wait for HTTPS to become active, then test every page, navigation item, internal link, external link, image, downloadable file, redirect, and form. Inspect desktop and mobile layouts.

Confirm that the deployed version matches the newest commit on the documented GitHub production branch.

Human verification: Open the public root and www addresses (as applicable) yourself. Verify HTTPS, critical navigation, forms, assets, and mobile layouts. Do not call the publication complete based only on Codex's report.

Step 5 — Record the website's setup

Keep the following accessible in the repository documentation: website name/purpose; repository; production branch; Cloudflare Worker/project; temporary Cloudflare URL; all public addresses; runtime and build/deploy commands; required environment variable names only; external services; owner/reviewers; registrar; verified first deployment date; routine edit and rollback procedures.
understand:
Why Cloudflare? GitHub holds the complete source of the website, including its change history. Cloudflare builds and serves the approved production version. Codex assists with creating, checking, and configuring the work, but a human still approves consequential changes.

Why a temporary address first? You can see and test the hosted site before directing public visitors to it. This separates “does the deployment work?” from “does the public domain point to it?”

What is a domain? The human-readable address visitors type. A subdomain is a name within an existing domain; a root domain is the main registered name. DNS maps domain names to the services they use. Changing nameservers is a broader action than updating one website address: it changes which provider manages the domain's authoritative DNS records.
deep:
• Build configuration: framework, runtime version, build/deploy commands, Worker/project type, production-branch triggers and optional preview builds differ by site. Never assume one DLL site's commands apply everywhere.
  • Deployment provenance: verify the GitHub commit on the production branch matches the version running on Cloudflare.
  • DNS and services: a domain may also carry mail (MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC), domain verification, other subdomains, CAA and SRV entries, routes, redirects, and third-party integrations. Do not change nameservers casually.
  • Access and secrets: use individual member accounts, least-needed permissions, multi-factor authentication, and protected Cloudflare secrets/environment variables; never expose secret values in logs, prompts, or repositories.

title: Move an Existing Website to Cloudflare
do:
This path has more checkpoints because the existing site—and sometimes email and other services—must keep working during the change.

Important: Migration has two separate parts: (1) prepare/move hosting and (2) move the domain's authoritative DNS. Copying only the website records can break other domain services. Keep the old host available until the migration is verified and the owner approves retirement.

Step 1 — Gather essential information

Collect: website name; all public domains/subdomains; existing host and registrar; source files/repository; known production branch; current DNS records and nameservers; email service and MX/SPF/DKIM/DMARC records; forms, databases, analytics, redirects, scheduled jobs and other external services; required environment variable/secret names; and authorized migration approver. Ask Codex to identify unknown technical details first; ask the DLL IT contact when details remain unknown. Do not cancel existing hosting. If no GitHub repository exists, the migration includes creating a dedicated one in the approved DLL GitHub organization.

Step 2 — Request a read-only audit

Open the existing project in Codex. If no local project exists, create a clearly named empty project folder. Replace placeholders in the prompt below.

Help me prepare to move the existing DLL website at <PUBLIC WEBSITE ADDRESS> to the shared DLL Cloudflare account. Its source is located at <GITHUB REPOSITORY OR CURRENT SOURCE LOCATION>.

Begin with a read-only audit. Identify the framework, required runtime version, build process, hosting requirements, forms, databases, server-side functions, redirects, environment variables, external services, and current deployment method. Check the current public website and identify every hostname it uses.

Do not modify files, create Cloudflare resources, change DNS, publish anything, or expose secret values. Give me:

    1. A plain-language migration plan
    2. A list of required access and approvals
    3. A list of risks or possible service interruptions
    4. A list of DNS and non-website services that must be preserved
    5. A rollback plan

Review the audit with the website owner. If the site isn't in GitHub, request a repository plan:

Prepare this website to use GitHub as its complete source of truth. Propose a clearly named repository under the approved DLL GitHub organization and identify anything that must not be committed.

Do not create the repository, upload files, or change the live website until I approve the plan.

Only after approval should Codex create/populate that repository.

Step 3 — Prepare and test a Cloudflare-compatible version

Prepare this website for Cloudflare hosting using the safest Cloudflare product for its existing framework. Prefer Cloudflare Workers when the website is compatible, but do not change frameworks unnecessarily.

Preserve the website's current appearance, URLs, metadata, redirects, forms, accessibility, and search-engine behavior.

Add only the configuration and source changes needed for Cloudflare. Store no credentials in the repository. Use Cloudflare secrets or environment variables for sensitive values.

Work on a separate Git branch. Run all available checks and create a local preview. Do not push, merge, deploy, change DNS, or affect the public website.

Then ask Codex to test and compare the prepared version:

Test the prepared website completely. Check every page, navigation item, image, downloadable file, internal link, external link, redirect, form, desktop layout, and mobile layout.

Compare it with the current public website and list any differences. Do not publish anything.

Human checkpoint: Inspect the preview and correct discrepancies.

Step 4 — Confirm Cloudflare member access

A shared-account Cloudflare Super Administrator invites the maintainer under Manage Account → Members, assigning only permissions needed for the relevant domain and project. The maintainer accepts with their own account and enables multi-factor authentication. Never share the Cloudflare owner password.

Step 5 — Prepare DNS without changing nameservers yet

Add the domain to Cloudflare using a full DNS setup. Cloudflare assigns nameservers, but do not yet change them at the registrar. Inventory, import, and compare existing records, including A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain verification, CAA, SRV, forms, newsletters, analytics, and other subdomains. Mail-related records normally remain DNS only, not proxied.

Compare the existing authoritative DNS records for <DOMAIN> with the records prepared in Cloudflare.

Pay special attention to email, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, verification records, subdomains, redirects, and third-party services.

Give me an exact record-by-record comparison and identify anything missing, conflicting, or unsafe. Do not add, delete, or modify DNS records. Do not change nameservers.

Stop here until the DNS inventory and comparison have been checked and agreed complete by a responsible person. A Codex response alone is not adequate authorization to proceed.

Step 6 — Test a temporary Cloudflare deployment

Prepare to deploy the approved website to a temporary Cloudflare address without changing the public domain.

Use the repository's existing configuration when available. If no Cloudflare configuration exists, propose a unique Worker or project name based on the website's name.

Show me every Cloudflare resource, command, environment variable, and setting you intend to create. Wait for my approval before creating or changing anything.

After approval:

Create the approved temporary deployment, wait for it to finish, and test the temporary Cloudflare address.

Compare it with the current public website. Do not connect the public domain or modify its DNS.

Open and verify the temporary address yourself.

Step 7 — Change nameservers carefully

If DNSSEC is enabled, follow Cloudflare's procedure to disable it before the nameserver change and re-enable after Cloudflare is active. At the registrar, replace, rather than append to, the old nameserver entries with the two nameservers Cloudflare assigned. Don't cancel hosting. Wait until Cloudflare marks the domain Active.

Check whether <DOMAIN> now uses the assigned Cloudflare nameservers and whether the Cloudflare zone is active.

Verify the website, email-related DNS records, important subdomains, HTTPS, and external services. Do not change the website or connect the new Cloudflare deployment yet.

The old website should still function via the copied DNS records at this stage.

Step 8 — Connect the approved deployment to the public domain

Only after DNS is active and the temporary site has passed testing:

Prepare to connect the approved Cloudflare deployment to <DOMAIN> and, if required, <WWW.DOMAIN>.

Check for existing DNS records, redirects, custom domains, or Worker routes that conflict with these hostnames.

Show me exactly which records or routes must change. Confirm that the old hosting configuration and rollback information have been preserved. Do not make the change until I explicitly approve it.

After reviewing the proposed cutover:

I approve the domain connection. Connect the approved Cloudflare deployment to <DOMAIN> and <WWW.DOMAIN>, wait for HTTPS certificates to become active, and perform a complete public test.

Do not delete or cancel the old hosting service.

A Worker Custom Domain can create the necessary DNS record/certificate, but the Cloudflare zone must already be active.

Step 9 — Verify before considering the migration finished

Verify: root domain; www if used; HTTPS; all public pages; navigation; redirects; images; downloads; forms; desktop/mobile; email delivery; important subdomains; analytics and other integrations. Keep old hosting until the owner approves the completed migration and the new deployment remains stable for an agreed period. Document repository, branch, build, deployment, domains, owners, and the rollback procedure.
understand:
Why so many checkpoints? A website has more moving pieces than the visible pages. Hosting runs the site; DNS directs visitors (and often mail) to services. Moving one without confirming the other can make a seemingly successful website migration interrupt email, verification, or subdomains.

Why compare the old and new site? A successful build doesn't prove that forms, redirects, SEO metadata, accessibility, downloads, integrations, and mobile layouts still work. The comparison helps reveal differences before public cutover.

Why keep the old host? The rollback plan needs to remain viable while the new site is being verified.
deep: Explore: authoritative versus cached DNS; record-by-record inventory; DNSSEC; Cloudflare zones and Worker routes; HTTP redirects and TLS certificates; server-side functions and secrets; dependency inventories; staged deployment and rollback design. These are optional explanations, not permission to bypass approval gates.

title: Publish an Approved Update
do:
Use this when an existing Cloudflare-hosted DLL website has a reviewed change ready to release.

  1. Confirm that the correct pull request is approved and the repository's required checks passed. Ensure the pull request targets the documented production branch.
  2. Use this instruction, recommended for this workflow:
This pull request is approved.

Confirm that all required checks passed, merge it into the documented production branch, and monitor the Cloudflare production deployment.

When publishing finishes, verify that the deployed Git commit matches the merged GitHub commit. Test the changed page, navigation, images, links, forms, HTTPS, desktop layout, and mobile layout.

Report the final GitHub commit and all live website addresses.
  1. Open every official public address yourself. Verify the updated content, navigation, links, images, forms, HTTPS, and desktop/mobile layouts. For example, check both https://writeai.center and https://www.writeai.center for the WRITE AI Center as examples, not addresses to assume for every DLL site.
  2. If deployment fails, do not manually upload a different production copy, disconnect GitHub, force-push, or overwrite another person's work. Go to Manage & Troubleshoot → Deployment Failed. If the published change is faulty, use the Revert a Published Change guide; changes and rollbacks must remain in GitHub.
understand: A pull request supports review; a merge integrates the approved change into the production branch; an automated Cloudflare build can publish that branch. The goal is for GitHub and the public website to represent the same approved code.
deep: Cloudflare Workers Builds may automatically build/deploy from the production branch, and can support preview builds for other branches. Compare Git commit identifiers when verifying which version is live. Build/test/lint commands are repository-specific.

title: Manage & Troubleshoot
intro: Maintain your website and find safe solutions.
do: Maintain your website and find safe solutions.

title: Update my existing website
do:
Use this when your existing site is already connected to the normal DLL GitHub-to-Cloudflare publishing workflow.

  1. Open the correct local website project in Codex. Ask Codex to verify the repository, production branch, Cloudflare project, build and test commands, domains, and deployment process—without changing anything.
  2. Ask Codex to check for unfinished work, safely get the latest approved production version, and create a separate branch, preserving everyone else's work.
  3. Describe the requested change clearly: affected page, exact text, images, links, placement, appearance, and what must not change.
  4. Review Codex's plan before edits, then review a local preview, tests, changed files, mobile layout, links, images, and forms before publication.
  5. After your review, have Codex commit only the relevant files on the separate branch, push it, and open a pull request. Do not merge or publish until approved.
  6. After authorized approval, merge to the documented production branch; watch Cloudflare build and deploy; check every public address yourself.

Complete guided instructions and copyable prompts: Build Your Website → Update an Existing Website.
Publishing checkpoint: Publish Your Website → Publish an Approved Update.
understand: A safe website update moves through stages: working branch → preview and review → pull request → approved production branch → Cloudflare deployment → human verification. Codex helps execute tasks; GitHub maintains approved source and review history; Cloudflare serves the live website.
deep: Review production-branch configuration, check results, the merged commit and the deployed commit. the DLL workflow uses main only as a normal default, not a guarantee for every project. It gives npm run build, npm test, and npm run lint for the WRITE AI Center website as examples, not universal commands.

title: Where is my website update?
do:
Do It — quick checks (diagnostic based on the DLL workflow's workflow)

Choose the closest description:

  • I asked Codex to make a change but can't see a pull request. Check the correct repository's Pull requests page and any active Codex task. the DLL workflow requires a separate branch, commit, push, and pull request after the local change is approved; a completed local change is not necessarily a GitHub PR.
  • I can see a pull request, but the live website hasn't changed. Verify that the PR was approved and merged to the documented production branch. An open PR alone should not change the public website.
  • The pull request was merged, but the website hasn't changed. Go to My changes aren't appearing on the live site.
  • I'm unsure which repo or website Codex edited. Use the read-only verification prompt below before making another change.

Codex prompt — verify the project

Verify that this folder is connected to the correct GitHub repository for <WEBSITE NAME>.

Identify the production branch, Cloudflare project or Worker, build commands, test commands, public domains, and current deployment workflow.

Do not change files, install software, commit, push, merge, deploy, or publish anything. Give me a plain-language summary of what you find.

Understand: A branch holds proposed work; a pull request requests review; a merge joins an approved change to the production branch; a deployment makes that version available at a public address.

Go Deeper: Confirm the repository URL, PR number, merge status, production-branch name, merge commit identifier, and Cloudflare deployment's linked Git commit before deciding what action is needed.
understand: A branch holds proposed work; a pull request requests review; a merge joins an approved change to the production branch; a deployment makes that version available at a public address.
deep: Confirm the repository URL, PR number, merge status, production-branch name, merge commit identifier, and Cloudflare deployment's linked Git commit before deciding what action is needed.

title: Check that my website is working
do:
Open every official production address, including the root domain and www if applicable. Check:

Done means: Codex reports a successful verification and an authorized person has opened and checked the live website. Don't assume a green deployment indicator proves every feature works.
understand: A completed deployment is not the same as a verified website. A site can build successfully but still have a broken image, form, DNS entry, or mobile interaction.
deep: Compare the production deployment's Git commit with the latest approved production-branch commit. Inspect relevant deployment logs and the repository's existing test commands; do not impose another site's build/test configuration.

title: Find the important details about my website
do:
Keep these details in your website's documentation:

  • Website name and purpose
  • GitHub repository and production branch
  • Cloudflare Worker/project name and temporary Cloudflare address
  • Public addresses, including necessary subdomains
  • Required runtime version; build and deploy commands
  • Required environment-variable names (never secret values)
  • External services, forms, analytics, and integrations
  • Website owner and publication reviewers
  • Domain registrar
  • First verified production deployment date
  • Routine editing and rollback procedures

If you're unsure, start with the DLL workflow's read-only project verification prompt from Where is my website update?. If access, ownership, or domain details remain unknown, ask the person responsible for the site's infrastructure. Ask your authorized DLL IT contact for help with unknown migration information.
understand: You need to know which repository is authoritative and which Cloudflare deployment serves it. A project's temporary Cloudflare address and its public custom domain may be different, but should lead to the correct approved website.
deep: Separate public configuration facts (repository, production branch, project identifier) from protected configuration (API tokens, credentials, customer/research data, private keys). Names of required variables can be documented; their values belong in Cloudflare secrets/protected environment configuration—not in public GitHub code or Codex prompts.

title: My changes aren't appearing on the live site
do:
Symptom: “I requested an update and Codex says it finished, but my public website still shows the old content.”

Guided diagnostic (decision path; check facts before making changes)

Question 1. Was a pull request opened?

  • No / not sure: Inspect the correct repository and working branch; use Where is my website update?. Codex may have prepared work without pushing it.
  • Yes: Continue.

Question 2. Was the PR approved and merged into the documented production branch?

  • No: The change has not followed the DLL workflow's public release stage. Arrange authorized review and approval; do not bypass the review.
  • Yes: Continue.

Question 3. Did Cloudflare produce a successful production deployment for that merge commit?

  • No / failed: Use My Cloudflare deployment failed.
  • Not sure: Check the website's Cloudflare deployment history and compare its Git commit with GitHub.
  • Yes: Continue.

Question 4. Are you checking the correct public address and page?

  • Check both root and www if used, and confirm the correct route/page. If the production deployment is successful and matches the commit, but the old content remains, collect the URLs, commit identifiers, and deployment details for diagnosis. Do not randomly change DNS or deploy a separate manual copy.
understand: There are multiple places for a change to stop: before a PR, before merge, during Cloudflare build/deploy, or after deployment when you're viewing a different address. Asking where it stopped is more useful than re-running every step.
deep: Compare: requested change → branch → PR → merge commit → production branch → Cloudflare deployment commit → public hostname. This is a diagnostic sequence, not authorization to force-push or manually override production.

title: My Cloudflare deployment failed
do:
Symptom: “Cloudflare shows a failed deployment / build error.”

Stop and protect existing work. Do not delete files, overwrite other people's work, force-push, disconnect GitHub, modify public domains, or deploy an independent manual copy.

Codex prompt — failed deployment

Stop and protect the existing work.

Do not delete files, overwrite another person’s work, force-push, disconnect GitHub, modify the public domains, or deploy a separate manual copy.

Read the complete build or deployment error, identify the cause, and explain the safest correction in plain language. Show me the proposed changes and wait for approval.

What to do next: Obtain the complete build/deployment error and the relevant project and commit identifiers. Review Codex's proposed diagnosis and corrections with the authorized person before approving any source changes. Keep fixes in GitHub's reviewed workflow, then verify the deployment and website again.

What counts as resolved: The intended production commit successfully deploys to the correct Cloudflare project and the live website passes human checks.
understand: A failed build means Cloudflare could not produce or publish the intended version. The error might involve project-specific configuration or source code; the DLL workflow does not provide a complete catalogue of error codes or prescribe specific one-size-fits-all fixes.
deep: Codex should inspect the actual project's build/deploy commands, runtime version, required environment-variable names, connection to the production branch, and logs before proposing a change. Any new troubleshooting catalogue must be tested against real DLL projects and kept separate from the DLL workflow's verified general safety procedure.

title: A published change broke my website
do:
Symptom: “The bad change is already live.”

Stop further uncontrolled publication. Identify the precise merged change; ask Codex to prepare a GitHub revert of only that change, preview and test the revert, and seek approval before merging/publishing it.

Codex prompt — proposed revert

Find the exact merged website change that caused the problem.

Prepare a GitHub revert that reverses only that change. Test the revert locally and show me exactly what it will change.

Do not merge or publish the revert until I approve it.

After approval, follow the normal reviewed GitHub production workflow and check the repaired live site. Do not delete history, force-push the production branch, or replace Cloudflare with a separate uploaded copy.
understand: A GitHub revert creates a new change that undoes a previous change while preserving the review and version history. That helps GitHub and Cloudflare remain in sync; it is different from deleting the previous version or directly replacing files in Cloudflare.
deep: The hardest part is accurately identifying the causing merge commit and confirming the proposed revert only affects the intended work. If later changes depend on the faulty change, pause for a case-specific assessment rather than applying a blind revert.

title: My domain or www address is not working
do:
Symptom: “The site works at one address but not another,” or “The website/domain stopped working during migration.”

  1. Confirm the exact hostname that should work: root domain (example.org), www.example.org, or a specified subdomain.
  2. Check whether the issue affects the temporary Cloudflare deployment address, public custom domain, or both. Do not change settings yet.
  3. Confirm whether the domain's Cloudflare zone has been reported Active and which nameservers are configured only if this is part of a migration/new-domain setup.
  4. For a domain migration, verify that the full DNS inventory—including A/AAAA/CNAME, MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, verification, CAA, SRV, and other service records—was preserved before nameservers were changed. Email and unrelated services may be affected by incomplete DNS migration.
  5. Ask Codex for a read-only check; have the responsible person review the findings before changing DNS, routes, or domain settings.

Codex prompt — DNS records comparison

Compare the existing authoritative DNS records for <DOMAIN> with the records prepared in Cloudflare.

Pay special attention to email, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, verification records, subdomains, redirects, and third-party services.

Give me an exact record-by-record comparison and identify anything missing, conflicting, or unsafe. Do not add, delete, or modify DNS records. Do not change nameservers.

Codex prompt — inspect a domain connection before altering it

Prepare to connect the approved Cloudflare deployment to <DOMAIN> and, if required, <WWW.DOMAIN>.

Check for existing DNS records, redirects, custom domains, or Worker routes that conflict with these hostnames.

Show me exactly which records or routes must change. Confirm that the old hosting configuration and rollback information have been preserved. Do not make the change until I explicitly approve it.

Do not casually change nameservers. They determine the DNS provider for an entire domain, not merely the website. Preserve the old host until migration is verified and stable for an agreed period.
understand: Domain = memorable public address; DNS = records that route that address and related services; nameservers = indicate which DNS provider is authoritative; custom domain/route = tells Cloudflare which site should respond at a hostname. Some domain changes can disrupt email even when the website itself appears fine.
deep: For full DNS setup, records must be inventoried and reviewed before a registrar nameserver change. the DLL workflow also addresses DNSSEC during cutover, waiting for Cloudflare Active status, HTTPS certificate activation, root and www verification, and not changing nameservers for a subdomain when the parent domain is already managed by Cloudflare. Follow Publish → Move an Existing Website for that complete high-risk procedure.

title: An image, link, page, download, or form is broken
do:
Choose a symptom:

  • Image or download missing: Identify the exact page URL, asset URL (if known), and whether the issue appears in the preview, temporary deployment, or live site.
  • Link or navigation broken: Record the source page, target URL, and whether the problem is a wrong destination, missing page, or failed redirect.
  • Mobile layout looks wrong: Record the page, device width or phone model, and what appears incorrectly. Compare desktop and mobile previews.
  • Form isn't working: Record the form page and expected behavior, the actual failure, and whether delivery/integration is affected. Never include submissions, passwords, personal data, API keys, or secrets in Codex prompts.
  • Unknown issue: Describe the observed behavior and when it started. Start with a read-only audit and testing plan.

Codex prompt — test a proposed website change

Check this change completely. Run all build, test, lint, accessibility, and validation commands already provided by the repository.

Open the local preview and inspect the affected page at desktop and mobile sizes. Also verify navigation, images, links, forms, and the other public pages.

Show me the preview and give me a plain-language summary of every file changed. Do not commit, push, merge, deploy, or publish anything.

If the issue requires a change, return to the normal branch → preview/test → pull request → approval → merge/deployment → live verification path. If a faulty change is already public and rollback is required, use A published change broke my website.
understand: Testing the local preview, temporary Cloudflare address, and live domain separately tells you whether the problem was introduced during editing or appears only after deployment. This is a diagnostic distinction, not proof of any particular cause.
deep: Review repository-specific tests and external-service dependencies. the DLL workflow calls for checking forms, analytics, redirects, downloadable files, accessibility, and mobile layouts but does not specify provider-by-provider solutions for broken integrations. Those must be added and verified later if needed.

title: I'm not sure what's wrong
do:
If you cannot identify the relevant category, begin with these facts:

  • Which site? Website name, its public address, and GitHub repo if known.
  • What were you trying to do? Describe the intended change or operation.
  • What happened instead? Include exact non-sensitive error text or a redacted screenshot.
  • Where? Codex, GitHub, Cloudflare, registrar, or the public site.
  • When? Before editing, during review, during deployment, or after publication.
  • What is affected? Only the preview, the public site, a form, a subdomain, email, or other services.

Before acting, ask Codex to inspect the configuration, repository, deployment process, and available error details without writing or publishing. Do not send secrets, private research data, subscribers' information, or authentication codes. Seek the website owner's or publication approver's permission for changes as required.

optional read-only diagnostic prompt ():

Help me identify why <WEBSITE NAME> is not behaving as expected.

What I expected: <EXPECTED RESULT>
What happened: <OBSERVED RESULT OR NON-SENSITIVE ERROR>
Affected address/page: <URL>

First perform a read-only inspection of the correct repository, documented production branch, relevant build/deployment status, and publicly accessible behavior. Explain the likely stage of failure, what evidence supports it, and what information is still missing.

Do not edit files, commit, push, merge, change DNS, expose or request secret values, or deploy. Propose a safe next check and wait for my approval.

Know when to stop: If the problem involves public service interruption, email/DNS, credentials, private research data, or a shared infrastructure change, stop experimenting and involve the authorized maintainer.
understand:
Why this matters

This task is part of the shared DLL workflow: Codex helps prepare or inspect work, GitHub keeps the approved website source and review history, and Cloudflare publishes the approved production branch. Use the steps in Do It when ready, and review the checks and approvals before changing anything public.
deep:
Technical context

Every DLL website can have its own repository, build commands, branch, Cloudflare project, domain records, and connected services. Before applying a technical instruction, confirm those details for this particular site. Keep credentials and unpublished sensitive information out of prompts and the repository. When a change affects shared services, review the impact and rollback plan before approval.
